steps.body: An inequality like y > 2x − 1 doesn't pick a line — it picks a SIDE. Its solutions are every point whose coordinates make the statement true: a whole half-plane of them. To find which side, you don't need theory. Pick any point not on the boundary and ask it.
Interrogate the easiest witness on the plane.

widget.prompt: Plot the classic test point — the origin — and we'll ask it about y > 2x − 1.

pointErrors.feedback: That's (1, 1) on these axes — the origin is where both labels read 0, bottom-left.

widget.missFeedback: The origin sits where x = 0 and y = 0 — the bottom-left corner.
widget.successFeedback: (0, 0): the cheapest arithmetic on the plane. Substituting zeros kills every term with a variable.

predict.prompt: When we substitute (0, 0) into y > 2x − 1, the statement becomes…
predict.reveal: 0 > 2·0 − 1 is 0 > −1 — TRUE. So the origin is a solution, and the entire origin side of the line is the solution region. One point's testimony convicts a whole half-plane.

explanationVariants: Substituting (0, 0) gives 0 > −1, which is true, so the origin's side is the solution side.
The origin satisfies the inequality, so shading goes on the origin's side of the boundary.

widget.prompt: The test gave 0 > −1 (true). Which side of y = 2x − 1 gets shaded?

options.label: The side containing (0, 0)
options.feedback: A true verdict means the witness lives in the region — shade its side.

options.label: The opposite side
options.feedback: Opposite shading is for a FALSE verdict — the witness would live outside.

options.label: Both sides
options.feedback: An inequality with > picks exactly one half-plane, never both.

steps.body: Why one witness suffices: crossing the boundary flips the comparison, and NOT crossing it can't. All points on one side vote the same way. So a single test point speaks for its whole side — choose (0, 0) whenever the boundary misses it, because zeros make the arithmetic trivial.

explanationVariants: (0, 0) in y < x − 2 gives 0 < −2, false, so the solution side is the one AWAY from the origin.
The origin fails the inequality, so shading goes on the non-origin side.

widget.prompt: Test (0, 0) in y < x − 2. What happens?

options.label: 0 < −2 is false — shade the side away from the origin
options.feedback: A failed witness means the region is the OTHER side.

options.label: 0 < −2 is true — shade the origin's side
options.feedback: Check the arithmetic: is zero less than negative two? No.

options.label: The test breaks — pick another point
options.feedback: The test worked perfectly; it just answered 'not this side.'

steps.body: Compute a boundary value to test against.
explanationVariants: At (3, 4): 2·3 − 1 = 5 and 4 > 5 is false, so (3, 4) is not a solution of y > 2x − 1.
The right side evaluates to 5 at x = 3; the point's y = 4 doesn't exceed it.

widget.prompt: For y > 2x − 1: what does the right side equal at x = 3?

commonErrors.feedback: That's the point's y, not the expression's value: 2·3 − 1 = 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Evaluate the right side at x = 3: 2·3 − 1 = 5. That 5 is the boundary height the inequality compares y against.

explanationVariants: (0, 0) lies ON y = 2x, so it can't testify; any off-line point like (1, 0) works: 0 > 2 is false, so shade the other side.
A witness on the boundary is useless — pick (1, 0), get 0 > 2 false, and shade the side not containing it.
hints: Substitute (0, 0) into y = 2x — where does it land?
A point ON the boundary can't pick a side. Choose any point off the line, like (1, 0).

widget.prompt: For y > 2x, why can't (0, 0) be the test point — and what do you do?

options.label: It's on the boundary — use a different point
options.feedback: On-boundary witnesses are neutral — off-line ones still convict a side.

options.label: Zeros make the arithmetic wrong
options.feedback: Zeros make arithmetic EASY — the problem is location, not computation.

options.label: You must graph instead
options.feedback: A sketch is optional — any off-boundary point testifies just as well, no picture required.

steps.body: One point speaks for its whole side.
takeaways: An inequality's solutions fill a half-plane.
Test one off-boundary point: true → shade its side; false → shade the other.
(0, 0) is the witness of choice — unless it's on the line.
